title: Mackerel Cove report recognized
text:
A project that examined Jamestown’s vulnerable coastline has earned awards for four college students from the Rhode Island chapter of the American Society of Landscape Architects.
The report by the University of Rhode Island, “A Vision for Jamestown: Reimagining the Mackerel & Sheffield Coves Waterfront,” was led by professor Hongbing Tan. It was the capstone project for 19 students in URI’S Department of Landscape Architecture with help from two engineering undergraduates.
Spencer Asofsky, Stephanie Nordhoff and Tim Purcell all received a merit award in planning and analysis. Madeline Ashenfelter received a merit award in communication.
“These awards are significant because they highlight the next generation of landscape architects, elevate high-quality academic work to the broader professional community, and showcase contributions that respond to Rhode Island’s pressing environmental and coastal challenges,” Tang said. “For students, the awards affirm that their academic work meets real-world expectations.”
The two coves on opposite sides of Beavertail Road, according to the report, are among the most vulnerable coastal areas in Rhode Island. Storms severely damage the dune system at Mackerel Cove, wash sand across Beavertail Road, and repeatedly close the only road connecting the northern and southern portions of Conanicut Island.
The engineering students conducted a year-long technical study that included surveying the beach, mapping storm inundation and modeling the flood risk. The team then developed strategies designed to rehabilitate the ecology, restore the dunes and control flooding. The partnership, beyond an academic exercise, reflected real-world challenges.
“Coastal resilience requires solutions that address both environmental processes and human needs,” Tang said.
“What surprised me most was how much more effective designs become when we stop trying to control nature and start listening to it,” Nordhoff added. “Coastal resilience depends on working with natural dynamics, not against them.”
The course began when the students met with municipal officials in January 2025 followed by a visit to Mackerel Cove to understand the concerns related to flooding, erosion and access. The team also hosted a community workshop that drew nearly 60 residents with an online survey to reach a broader audience.
“Community members spoke with genuine affection for the cove’s character and peaceful atmosphere, which emphasized the importance of protecting its natural beauty while improving accessibility and long-term resilience,” Asofsky said.
Lisa Bryer, who headed the planning department for Jamestown during the project, said Tang and her students “did a wonderful job keeping the community involved in the project.”
“When people can be informed and provide meaningful input, they feel heard and empowered, which is a critical element of a successful democracy,” Bryer said.
The final report provides a set of conceptual design options for improving coastal resilience at the coves. From conservation strategies to visionary infrastructure solutions, the ideas range from accessible pathways and habitat restoration to engineered interventions, including artificial reefs and elevated roadways.
“Importantly, our strategies operate at both ecological and social levels,” Asofsky said.
“Interventions intended to improve habitat and shoreline stability also structured safer, more accessible ways for people to engage with the waterfront while preserving the site’s character.”
“Given the urgency of storm damage and sea-level rise,” Tang added, “the students’ work offers valuable starting points for future resilience investments.”
Anne Kuhn-Hines, who chaired the town’s conservation commission during the project, called the report “comprehensive, creative, inspiring and informative.”
“I am thoroughly impressed,” she said. “What a wonderful gift.”
The report was supported by the Rhode Island Sea Grant.
